quotes.text: Indicators go stale fast because an attacker can swap a domain or rebuild a file overnight, while a TTP lasts longer. Because changing a habit is harder than changing an address.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains clearly why behaviour-based intelligence outlasts single indicators.

quotes.text: Real signal shows up when several indicators point at the same place at the same time. And that pattern is what turns noise into a lead.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Practical rule against treating one indicator as proof.

quotes.text: What makes the story worth telling is that nobody found a single smoking gun. Investigators found overlapping details, and those overlaps did the work.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Captures the core idea of infrastructure analysis in two sentences.

quotes.text: Fourteen days of passive DNS gives you a snapshot, while unlimited history gives you a timeline, and infrastructure analysis depends on seeing how connections changed over months.

chapters.title: Threat actors: who is behind the attack

takeaways: Threat intelligence adds context to alerts: it explains who is behind an attack, what they want and which infrastructure they use.
A single indicator of compromise is weak evidence; real signal appears when several indicators, actor profiles and shared infrastructure point to the same operation.
Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence now lives inside Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel, so analysts enrich incidents and follow connections outward from one entity.
hook: Security alerts tell you something broke, but not who is behind it or what they will touch next. This episode explains Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence for beginners and security-curious IT pros: indicators of compromise, threat actor naming and infrastructure chaining. You will learn how one suspicious domain can expose an entire criminal operation.
